name: Cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida, upper Amazon
summary: People in southeast Ecuador were using cacao about 5,300 years ago, the earliest evidence of cacao use in the Americas.
description: Around 5,300 years ago people at Santa Ana-La Florida in southeast Ecuador used cacao, shown by starch grains, theobromine residues and ancient DNA recovered from their artefacts. The authors argue this is the earliest evidence of T. cacao use in the Americas. Whether the people domesticated the plant or gathered pods from wild trees is still debated.

impact.note: One society in one region used it (reach 1); a new food and drink plant added to an existing diet (depth 1); later cacao use elsewhere may descend from upper Amazon use, but no source here ties it to this community, so generativity stays at 1.

date.label: c. 3350 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida, Ecuador, is dated to about 5,300 years ago, which is about 3350 BCE by the 1950 convention.

evidence.supports: dating from approximately 5,300 years ago recovered from the Santa Ana-La Florida (SALF) site in southeast Ecuador

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Coordinates of Santa Ana-La Florida: the place is given as the town of Palanda, the canton centre near the site, because no fetched source gave site coordinates.
Whether the upper Amazon people domesticated cacao or only gathered wild pods; the genomic domestication signal in Central America dates to about 3,600 years ago.
How and when cacao reached Mesoamerica, and whether Mesoamerican chocolate needs its own derived record.

research.note: The paper says that, to the authors' knowledge, these finds are the earliest evidence of cacao use in the Americas, where the tree is native; no earlier use is known anywhere.
